title: What can you say about oat beta-glucan in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 3 wordings for oat beta-glucan; the strongest is "Helps maintain normal blood cholesterol levels" (strong, 3-10 g beta-glucan a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Lowers cholesterol, or reduces heart disease risk, outside FDA's authorized wording and conditions", and keep "When taken with a meal, helps reduce the rise in blood sugar after that meal" off Meta ads.

supported_wordings.wording: Helps maintain normal blood cholesterol levels.
supported_wordings.why: The EU authorizes maintenance of normal blood cholesterol at 3 g a day, and Health Canada lists LDL cholesterol lowering at 2-10 g a day.
supported_wordings.dose_details: EU: 3 g of beta-glucans a day from oats, oat bran, barley or barley bran, with at least 1 g per portion. Health Canada: 2-10 g a day for adults 18 and older for its LDL cholesterol use.
supported_wordings.form: Beta-glucan from oats, oat bran, barley or barley bran

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

supported_wordings.wording: When taken with a meal, helps reduce the rise in blood sugar after that meal.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada and the EU both accept it, but on clearly different dose measures (per day and per meal).
supported_wordings.dose_details: Health Canada: 2-10 g a day for adults, for healthy glucose metabolism within two hours after a meal. EU: at least 4 g of beta-glucans from oats or barley for each 30 g of available carbohydrates in the meal.

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

supported_wordings.meta_ads: Wording to avoid in Meta ads. On your site it is supported wording.

supported_wordings.wording: A source of fibre that helps support a healthy digestive system.
supported_wordings.why: One listed source, Health Canada, lists it, citing nutrition references.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Health Canada: 2-10 g a day for adults ('Source of fiber for the maintenance of good health'; 'Helps support and maintain a healthy digestive system').

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Lowers cholesterol, or reduces heart disease risk, outside FDA's authorized wording and conditions
wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule gives 'lowers cholesterol' as a disease claim (page 1015); heart disease risk belongs only in the authorized health claim (21 CFR 101.81).

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Lowers blood sugar in diabetes, or helps manage diabetes
When taken with a meal, helps reduce the rise in blood sugar after that meal.
wordings_to_avoid.why: Blood sugar is a health-condition claim on Meta, so this wording stays off Meta ads, as chromium's blood glucose wording does (library decision of 2026-10-15; Meta's ad policies were not read). It stays supported wording for pages.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

FDA authorized health claim: Soluble fiber from whole oats or barley and reduced risk of coronary heart disease

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
